Thank you Mr. O'Connell for the reply.

Would you please showing me on how to include the flexBayes library to my Splus workbench.

Thanks again,
Minh

______________________________________
From: Michael O'Connell [moconnel at tibco.com]
Sent: Thursday, December 02, 2010 8:25 AM
To: Dung Tran; snews
Subject: RE: [S] Can Splus call OPenBUgs or Winbugs?

S-PLUS 8.1 and above includes the FlexBayes library. This has an inbuilt
MCMC engine optimized for hierarchical general linear models. It also
has connectors for Winbugs. We have some ongoing work re connectivity to
Openbugs as well. FlexBayes is well documented and includes numerous
examples for calling out to Winbugs - these are primarily from the Life
Sciences and Financial Services industry.

Regards
Michael

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am running:
TIBCO Software Inc. Confidential Information
Copyright (c) 1988-2010 TIBCO Software Inc. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.
TIBCO Spotfire S+ Version 8.2.0 for Linux 2.6.9-34.EL, 64-bit : 2010


I have a moderately large data.frame:

dim(x)
[1] 1482525       7

One variable is some id.number (no.ind), I need to aggregate some
of the variables by this no.ind.  But the no.ind is not
duplicated very often, leaving me with a large number of unique
no.ind.

ttt.dupes <- duplicated(x$no.ind)
sum(!ttt.dupes)
[1] 1149097

Further more I don't want to do the same type of aggregation for
all variables.  I know I could use "by" or "aggregate" or friends
of the "apply" family, but with such a large number of classes it
is very slow.  I did it as following, but it is also very slow.

ttt.nrow.res <- sum(!ttt.dupes)
ttt.res <- data.frame(v1 = rep(NA, ttt.nrow.res),
                      v2 = rep(NA, ttt.nrow.res),
                      v3 = rep(NA, ttt.nrow.res),
                      v4 = rep(NA, ttt.nrow.res),
                      v4 = rep(NA, ttt.nrow.res),
                      v6 = rep(NA, ttt.nrow.res),
                      no.ind =  rep(NA, ttt.nrow.res))

j <- 1
i <- 1
for (j in 1:ttt.nrow.res) {
  if (ttt.dupes[i + 1] & i < nrow(x)) {
    first <- i
    while (ttt.dupes[i + 1] & i < nrowx(x)) i <- i + 1
    last <- i
    ttt.res[j, ] <-
      c(colSums(x[first:last,c("v1", "v2", "v3", "v4")],
                na.rm = F),
        colMeans(x[first:last,c("v5", "v6")],
                 weights = x[first:last, "v4"],
                 na.rm = F), x[first, "no.ind"])
    }
  else ttt.res[j, ] <- x[i, ]
  i <- i + 1
  j <- j + 1
  }

Thanks for any insights,

Gérald Jean
Conseiller senior en statistiques,
VP Actuariat et Solutions d'assurances,
Desjardins Groupe d'Assurances Générales
télephone            : (418) 835-4900 poste (7639)
télecopieur          : (418) 835-6657
courrier électronique: gerald.jean at dgag.ca

messages.body_plain:
Have you tried using the group{Means,Sums,Ranges,...}
family of functions?  Use them on one column of your
data.frame at a time to make a list of results, then
call data.frame on that list.  E.g.,
  > z <- data.frame(no.ind=rep(11:14,4:1), v1=sqrt(1:10), v2=2^(0:9))
  > tmp <- factor(z$no.ind) # supply levels= if order matters
  > result <- list(no.ind = levels(tmp))
  > result$v1 <- groupMeans(z$v1, group=tmp)
  > result$v2 <- groupSums(z$v2, group=tmp)
  > data.frame(result)
     no.ind       v1  v2
  11     11 1.536566  15
  12     12 2.443770 112
  13     13 2.914214 384
  14     14 3.162278 512
S+ has groupMeans, groupSums, groupVars, groupStdevs, groupMaxs,
groupMins, groupProds, groupAnys, groupAlls, and a related
subtractMeans().  They all have the optional arguments na.rm=
and weights= and all but the last has a repeats= argument.
They are fast.

Bill Dunlap
Spotfire, TIBCO Software
wdunlap tibco.com

messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Bill Dunlap and Samer Mouksassi for their replies,

yes I knew the "groupMeans" family of functions but I was worried, since I
needed different summary types (means and sums) for different variables
that the order wouldn't necessarily be the same for both functions, but
from Bill's suggestion ist seems the order is the same -- as an aside, it
would be nice if those functions outputted one column for the grouping
variable -- furthermore I didn't know a factor could have such a large
number of levels.  I ended up using the following code, and it worked
perfectly well and very fast.

ttt.fac <- factor(AutoVeh.pr.fusion$no.ind)
length(levels(ttt.fac))
[1] 1149097

ttt.gr <- groupSums(x = AutoVeh.pr.fusion[ ,c("clv.auto", "clv.res",
                      "clv.total", "prtotale")], group = ttt.fac)
colnames(ttt.gr)
ttt.me <- groupMeans(x = AutoVeh.pr.fusion[ ,c("lifetime",
"taux.de.succes")],
                     group = ttt.fac, weights = AutoVeh.pr.fusion$prtotale)
ttt.res <- data.frame(no.ind = levels(ttt.fac), ttt.gr, ttt.me)
dim(ttt.res)
[1] 1149097       7


Thanks again, very appreciated,

Gérald Jean
Conseiller senior en statistiques,
VP Actuariat et Solutions d'assurances,
Desjardins Groupe d'Assurances Générales

messages.subject: Re: Size limitations to data.frame
messages.body_plain:
There is no specific limit on the size of a data.frame.
The number of bytes in any column (numeric elements
use 8 bytes each) must be less than the largest possible
integer (2^63-1 on 64-bit S+ and 2^31-1 on 32-bit S+), but
the total amount of memory used must also be less than
this limit.  Many S+ functions will make several copies or
versions of the data.frame being used and all of those copies
or versions must fit into the general memory limit.
 
You can avoid the per-column memory limits by
using the bdFrame objects defined in library(bigdata),
but even then you will need to use 64-bit S+ if those
columns will be longer than 2^31-1 elements.

Bill Dunlap
Spotfire, TIBCO Software
wdunlap tibco.com
